extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (agents/attorneys), USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline staff, and attorneys handling USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural requirements, and sanctions applied by the USPTO (OED) when a registered practitioner is suspended, fails to cooperate with OED, or otherwise engages in misconduct; includes jurisdictional bases, rule citations, and the mechanics of suspension/probation and enforcement. Geared toward assessing practitioner conduct and determining disciplinary outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification duty upon suspension or other discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(a), '[w]ithin thirty days of being publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, subjected to probation, disbarred, or suspended by another jurisdiction, or being disciplinarily disqualified from participating in or appearing before any Federal program or agency, a practitioner subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Office shall notify the OED Director in writing of same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely written notice to the OED Director is required within 30 days. The Respondent timely sent a letter notifying OED of his California suspension (example of compliance). Failure to notify would implicate disciplinary rules and lead to further action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to respond to OED requests and lawful demands for information (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must cooperate with OED investigations and respond to lawful requests for information; failing to respond violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED may send Requests for Information and Evidence (RFIs) to the address on record (per 37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a)). Failure to respond within the given time (e.g., 30 days) can trigger 'Failure to Respond' notices, additional letters with short response windows, and can be charged as misconduct. Examples: OED mailed an RFI (Nov 6, 2013); Respondent received it but did not file a response, leading to successive notices and eventual disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly disobeying an obligation under the rules of a tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation consists of knowingly disobeying an obligation imposed by the rules of a tribunal; the Final Order cites failure to comply with court-ordered child or family support payments as an example causing a § 11.304(c) violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court-ordered obligations (e.g., child support) can fall within this prohibition when not complied with; such conduct is actionable before the USPTO when it reflects disobedience of tribunal-imposed obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice is proscribed by 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d); the Final Order treats both failure to pay court-ordered child support and failure to cooperate with OED as examples of such conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavior that undermines the administration of justice — whether through nonpayment of court obligations or obstruction of disciplinary inquiries — may be charged under § 11.804(d). This rule can be applied in multiple factual contexts as an aggravating basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO jurisdiction to discipline practitioners (35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) & 32; 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.20, 11.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over practitioner discipline under statutes and regulations: 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and implementing regulations at 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.20, and 11.26.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions provide the legal basis for OED investigations, settlement agreements, and issuance of Final Orders. They also authorize publication and imposition of sanctions. Practitioners should understand jurisdictional scope when assessing disciplinary exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures and remedies for noncompliance during probation (Order to Show Cause; suspension extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If OED believes a practitioner on probation failed to comply with the Agreement, Final Order, or rules, OED may issue an Order to Show Cause, send it to the practitioner's address of record, grant 15 days to respond, and, if noncompliance persists, request that the USPTO Director enter an immediate additional suspension for up to 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics: (1) OED issues Order to Show Cause; (2) serves it to the last address of record (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a)); (3) grants 15 days to respond; (4) after considering response, OED may deliver materials to the Director and request additional suspension. If suspended, seeking review does not stay the suspension. This sequence illustrates enforcement of probationary conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction types and conditional stays (suspension stayed by probation; duration and conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions available include suspension (here: six months) that may be stayed in its entirety by a period of probation (here: five years) subject to specified compliance conditions (e.g., satisfaction of state court arrearages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreed sanctions can combine immediate suspension with a stay conditioned on probation/compliance. Terms may specify when probation commences, what triggers revocation, and what remedial steps are required for completion (e.g., full compliance with state court orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of USPTO registration status upon suspension by another jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner is suspended by another jurisdiction, the OED Director may change the practitioner's USPTO registration status (example: from patent attorney to patent agent) as a consequence of the out-of-state suspension and notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's timely notice of California suspension resulted in OED changing his status. Practitioners should expect OED to adjust registration status in response to foreign-jurisdiction discipline or suspensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of disciplinary actions (OED FOIA Reading Room; Official Gazette)
rubrics_metrics.description: OED will electronically publish Final Orders in its FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette summarizing suspension/probation and the rule violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication is mandatory as part of discipline; notices typically include practitioner name, registration number, summary of violations and sanctions, and reference to statutory/regulatory bases. Practitioners should expect public disclosure of disciplinary outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disciplinary records in future proceedings and as aggravating factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.60 referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing prevents the Office from considering the record of the disciplinary proceeding (including the Final Order) in future complaints against the practitioner — as aggravating evidence, to rebut statements by the practitioner, or in connection with requests for reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior Final Order can be used by OED in later matters to increase discipline or counter representations; practitioners should be aware of collateral consequences of an entry on their disciplinary record.

rubrics_metrics.name: State court suspension for delinquent child support under California Rules of Court (Rule 9.22(a) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: California Rule 9.22(a) authorized transmission of names of attorneys delinquent in court-ordered child or family support for recommended suspension; Rule 9.22(b) provided that reinstatement requires notification from the State Bar that the name has been removed from the delinquency list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State procedures for suspension due to delinquent child support can trigger suspension from practice in that state and thereby create obligations to notify OED and may prompt USPTO action. The Final Order uses the California rule as the predicate for the state suspension that led to USPTO proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address of record service requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: OED mailed requests and letters to the address Respondent had provided pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a); service to the address of record is sufficient for notices and RFIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must maintain accurate address of record; OED's notices and RFIs sent to that address are effective even if not read. This affects timelines for response and can lead to discipline for nonresponse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating and aggravating considerations in discipline decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as absence of prior disciplinary history, timely self-reporting, expressions of remorse, cooperation, changes in underlying circumstances (e.g., support obligation reduced to zero), and payment plans toward arrears are considered as mitigating circumstances in determining sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order notes Respondent had no prior OED history, self-reported, expressed remorse, and was making payments toward arrears — these factors informed the negotiated sanction (suspension stayed by probation). Conversely, ongoing arrears and failure to respond to OED were aggravating factors. Practitioners should present mitigating facts where possible in settlement contexts.
